title: 1 Chronicles 7:30–40
context: The genealogy of Asher closes chapter 7. The first generation (Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and their sister Serah) and Beriah’s sons Heber and Malchiel match Genesis 46:17. The later names are not found elsewhere in Scripture, and some spellings appear to vary within the list itself (for example, Shomer in 7:32 and Shemer in 7:34); the text does not comment. The list ends with the number of men registered for war (7:40). Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: God’s faithfulness to the tribes includes the less prominent ones, and the record of “choice and mighty men of valor” honors their place among his people.

verses.text: The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, and Beriah. Serah was their sister.
verses.arminianNotes: Asher’s children are Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and their sister Serah. Arminian readers note that the list matches Genesis 46:17 and that a daughter is named among the sons. The Chronicler preserves the memory of women within the tribal record.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the agreement with Genesis 46:17 and Numbers 26:44–46, linking the returned community to the families who went down to Egypt. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as testimony to God’s faithfulness in preserving the tribe of Asher.

verses.text: The sons of Beriah: Heber and Malchiel, who was the father of Birzaith.
verses.arminianNotes: Beriah’s sons are Heber and Malchiel, the father of Birzaith. Arminian readers note the continuity with Genesis 46:17 and the link between a family and a place name. The record roots the tribe’s households in the land God gave them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the agreement with earlier lists and the connection between people and places. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as straightforward genealogy, with no point of doctrinal difference, and see in it God’s care for each family of Asher.

verses.text: Heber became the father of Japhlet, Shomer, Hotham, and Shua their sister.
verses.arminianNotes: Heber becomes the father of Japhlet, Shomer, Hotham, and their sister Shua. Arminian readers again note a daughter named in the line. The record presents women as part of the family’s identity, a quiet but consistent feature of these genealogies.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note Shua’s inclusion and the continuity of Heber’s family. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as family history and see in the naming of daughters a reminder that God’s covenant people include women as well as men.

verses.text: The sons of Japhlet: Pasach, Bimhal, and Ashvath. These are the children of Japhlet.
verses.arminianNotes: Japhlet’s sons are Pasach, Bimhal, and Ashvath. Arminian readers note that these names appear nowhere else in Scripture. Their preservation here shows the Chronicler’s concern to keep even little-known families within the record of God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the preservation of obscure names as evidence that God knows his people individually. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Asher’s family record and affirm that every household had a place among the people of God.

verses.text: The sons of Shemer: Ahi, Rohgah, Jehubbah, and Aram.
verses.arminianNotes: Shemer’s sons are named: Ahi, Rohgah, Jehubbah, and Aram. Arminian readers note that Shemer appears to be the Shomer of 7:32, a variation in spelling the text does not explain. They do not press such differences for conclusions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the apparent variation and treat it calmly, as common in ancient lists. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical detail and decline to build any theological point on the spelling of a name.

verses.text: The sons of Helem his brother: Zophah, Imna, Shelesh, and Amal.
verses.arminianNotes: The sons of Helem, Shemer’s brother, are Zophah, Imna, Shelesh, and Amal. Arminian readers note that Helem is not named earlier in the list, and some readers suggest he is Hotham of 7:32, though the text does not say so. They hold the link loosely.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the uncertainty and avoid forcing an identification. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Asher’s record, accept that some genealogical links remain unclear, and see no doctrinal question raised by the names.

verses.text: The sons of Zophah: Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri, Imrah,
verses.arminianNotes: Zophah’s sons begin a longer list: Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri, and Imrah. Arminian readers note the growth of Asher’s families across the generations. Each name stands for a household that lived and served within the covenant people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the multiplication of names as a sign of God’s blessing on the tribe. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical detail and see in the growing families a reflection of God’s promise to make Abraham’s descendants many.

verses.text: Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran, and Beera.
verses.arminianNotes: Zophah’s list continues with Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran, and Beera. Arminian readers note the length of the list, which honors a large family. The Chronicler keeps the record complete rather than summarizing, showing care for each person named.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the completeness of the list as reflecting God’s attention to every member of his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Asher’s genealogy and affirm that each name preserved has value before God.

verses.text: The sons of Jether: Jephunneh, Pispa, and Ara.
verses.arminianNotes: Jether’s sons are Jephunneh, Pispa, and Ara. Arminian readers note that Jether may be the Ithran of 7:37, though the text does not make the link. The name Jephunneh also appears elsewhere in Scripture for a different man, and they do not confuse the two.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the possible link with Ithran cautiously and note the recurrence of common names across tribes. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical detail and decline to build conclusions on uncertain identifications.

verses.text: The sons of Ulla: Arah, Hanniel, and Rizia.
verses.arminianNotes: Ulla’s sons are Arah, Hanniel, and Rizia. Arminian readers note that Ulla is otherwise unknown and that the text does not place him in the family tree. They accept the uncertainty and read the verse as part of a faithful, if incomplete, record.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the unclear link and do not speculate. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Asher’s genealogy, recognize that ancient lists can leave connections unstated, and affirm the value of preserving these names.

verses.text: All these were the children of Asher, heads of the fathers’ houses, choice and mighty men of valor, chief of the princes. The number of them listed by genealogy for service in war was twenty-six thousand men.
verses.arminianNotes: Asher’s heads of houses are “choice and mighty men of valor, chief of the princes,” with 26,000 listed for war. Arminian readers note the honor given to the tribe’s leaders and fighters. Their service is recorded as a real contribution to Israel’s life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the summary as a testimony to God’s preservation and blessing of a tribe that receives little attention elsewhere. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as closing Asher’s record with honor and see in it God’s faithfulness to all the tribes.
